AI.conclusion: SESNe preferentially occur in regions of intense, efficient star formation rather than environments with simply higher gas content, providing new constraints on their progenitor formation channels—either through very massive stars under top-heavy IMF or through interacting binaries whose formation is enhanced by turbulence-linked star formation efficiency boosts.

title: The progenitors of $z\gtrsim10$ JWST galaxies in the COLIBRE simulations
comment: 27 pages, 18 figures; submitted to MNRAS
summary: JWST has revealed a large population of luminous galaxies ($M_{\rm UV}\lesssim -20$) at redshifts $z \gtrsim 10$, widely interpreted as posing a challenge to models of galaxy formation within the $Λ$CDM cosmology. Here, we search for counterparts of the JWST galaxies in the COLIBRE simulations of galaxy formation. Although these simulations have not been tuned to reproduce any $z > 0$ observations, we find a population of COLIBRE galaxies with properties similar to those of the JWST galaxies, and trace them to their earliest evolutionary phases, $z\simeq25$, to investigate the onset of galaxy formation. We study the evolution of galaxy stellar masses, sizes, star formation rates, UV magnitudes, metallicities, central black hole masses, and molecular gas and dust content, finding good agreement with observationally inferred properties at $z > 10$, except for UV magnitudes and dust masses, which COLIBRE underpredicts and overpredicts, respectively. Our results indicate that the standard galaxy formation physics and $Λ$CDM cosmology adopted in COLIBRE are sufficient to reproduce a broad range of properties of the most extreme $z > 10$ JWST galaxies - including their compact sizes, stellar masses, gas content, and metallicities. We show that the discrepancies with the UV magnitudes and dust masses can both be attributed to the uncertain rate of grain growth at high redshift, possibly alongside a top-heavy stellar initial mass function. These findings provide strong evidence that the standard cosmological model can naturally explain even the most extreme galaxies in the early Universe.

AI.tldr: COLIBRE cosmological simulations, despite not being tuned to reproduce z>0 observations, naturally produce a population of luminous z>10 galaxies matching JWST observations across most properties (stellar masses, sizes, SFRs, metallicities, BH masses, gas content). Discrepancies in UV magnitudes and dust masses are attributed to uncertain grain growth rates and possibly a top-heavy IMF, providing evidence that ΛCDM with standard galaxy formation physics can explain the most extreme early Universe galaxies.
AI.motivation: JWST has discovered a large population of luminous galaxies at z>10 that have been widely interpreted as potentially challenging galaxy formation models within the standard ΛCDM cosmological framework. The authors aim to test whether standard physics in galaxy formation simulations can naturally reproduce these extreme early galaxies.
AI.method: The authors use the COLIBRE cosmological simulations of galaxy formation, which were not tuned to match any z>0 observations, to search for counterparts to the JWST z>10 galaxies. They trace these simulated galaxies back to their earliest evolutionary stages at z≃25 and compare their stellar masses, sizes, star formation rates, UV magnitudes, metallicities, central black hole masses, molecular gas, and dust content against observationally inferred properties.
AI.result: COLIBRE produces a population of galaxies with properties similar to the JWST galaxies at z>10, with good agreement across most properties including compact sizes, stellar masses, gas content, and metallicities. However, COLIBRE underpredicts UV magnitudes and overpredicts dust masses. Both discrepancies can be traced to the uncertain rate of grain growth at high redshift, possibly alongside a top-heavy stellar initial mass function.
AI.conclusion: Standard galaxy formation physics within the ΛCDM cosmology can naturally explain even the most extreme z>10 galaxies observed by JWST, implying that the early Universe galaxies do not pose a fundamental challenge to the standard cosmological model.

title: A comprehensive SKA Survey of lensing clusters and lensed galaxies
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKAII (AASKAII), 2026(arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no:AASKAII/Pandey-Pommier02. Advancing Astrophysics with the SKAII(AASKAII) outlines the transformative scientific advances that will be enabled by the SKA telescopes
summary: Galaxy clusters act as powerful gravitational lenses that provide a unique laboratory for studying the distribution of dark matter and the properties of faint background galaxies. In the radio regime, cluster lensing studies remain largely unexplored due to the intrinsically low surface density of background radio sources, which limits the number of detectable lensed systems and constrains the application of cluster-scale lensing to cosmological and astrophysical investigations. In this paper, we outline how the SKA will transform cluster lensing studies through its unprecedented sensitivity, angular resolution, and survey speed. These capabilities will enable dense sampling of lensed background radio sources and high-fidelity reconstruction of cluster mass distributions, while revealing a previously inaccessible population of faint ($μ$Jy-level) galaxies, primarily at $z \sim 1-5$. We focus on three key science goals: (i) constraining dark matter substructure in galaxy clusters through improved strong-lensing constraints, (ii) characterising the non-thermal baryonic components of the intracluster medium, and (iii) building statistically significant samples of $μ$Jy-level lensed galaxies to study star formation and active galactic nuclei activity across cosmic time (primarily at $z \sim 1-5$). Together, these advances will establish cluster-scale radio lensing as a powerful probe of structure formation and galaxy evolution in the SKA era.

AI.tldr: This paper outlines how the Square Kilometre Array (SKA) will transform galaxy cluster lensing studies in the radio regime through its unprecedented sensitivity, angular resolution, and survey speed, enabling three key science goals: constraining dark matter substructure, characterising non-thermal intracluster medium components, and building statistically significant samples of μJy-level lensed galaxies for studying star formation and AGN activity at z~1-5.
AI.motivation: Cluster-scale lensing in the radio regime remains largely unexplored because background radio sources have intrinsically low surface density, limiting detectable lensed systems and constraining cosmological and astrophysical applications of cluster lensing.
AI.method: The paper outlines how SKA's unprecedented sensitivity, angular resolution, and survey speed will enable dense sampling of lensed background radio sources and high-fidelity reconstruction of cluster mass distributions, providing access to faint μJy-level galaxies at z~1-5.
AI.result: The paper identifies three key science goals: (i) constraining dark matter substructure via improved strong-lensing constraints, (ii) characterising non-thermal baryonic components of the intracluster medium, and (iii) building statistically significant samples of μJy-level lensed galaxies to study star formation and AGN activity across cosmic time.
AI.conclusion: These advances will establish cluster-scale radio lensing as a powerful probe of structure formation and galaxy evolution in the SKA era.

title: Tracing gas outflows in molecular gas-rich galaxies with the SKA
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKAII (AASKAII), 2026(arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no:AASKAII/Pandey-Pommier01. Advancing Astrophysics with the SKAII (AASKAII) outlines the transformative scientific advances that will be enabled by the SKA telescopes
summary: Active galactic nuclei with powerful radio jets play a key role in galaxy evolution through their ability to regulate the cold gas reservoirs that fuel star formation. Jet-driven feedback can heat, compress, or expel atomic and molecular gas, thereby reshaping the interstellar medium and altering star formation efficiency. However, the physical coupling between AGN activity and the multi-phase interstellar medium remains poorly constrained, particularly in radio-loud systems where mechanical feedback and multiphase outflows are expected to dominate. SKA will provide major advances in the study of cold gas in AGN host galaxies through sensitive observations of H~{\sc i} emission and absorption, together with access to selected low-frequency molecular transitions within the SKA~1 frequency range, including OH, H$_2$CO, CH$_3$OH, and, at high redshift, low-$J$ transitions of CO, HCN, and HCO$^{+}$ in rare bright systems. Combined with radio continuum measurements, these tracers will provide direct constraints on gas mass, kinematics, turbulence, and inflow/outflow signatures, enabling detailed studies of feedback-regulated cold gas reservoirs in AGN environments. In this chapter, we examine how SKA1 observations of neutral hydrogen, complemented by molecular-line and radio continuum studies, can be used to quantify multiphase gas flows and feedback energetics in molecular-gas-rich radio galaxies. SKA surveys will enable population-level studies of AGN-driven feedback, providing a new framework for understanding how radio jets regulate the cold interstellar medium and star formation across cosmic time.

AI.tldr: This paper examines how SKA1 observations of neutral hydrogen (H I), complemented by molecular-line and radio continuum tracers, can quantify multiphase gas flows and feedback energetics in molecular-gas-rich radio galaxies, enabling population-level studies of how AGN-driven radio jets regulate cold gas reservoirs and star formation across cosmic time.
AI.motivation: Jet-driven feedback from active galactic nuclei (AGN) can heat, compress, or expel cold gas that fuels star formation, yet the physical coupling between AGN activity and the multi-phase interstellar medium remains poorly constrained, particularly in radio-loud systems where mechanical feedback and multiphase outflows dominate.
AI.method: The paper leverages SKA1's capabilities for sensitive observations of neutral hydrogen (H I) emission and absorption, together with low-frequency molecular transitions (OH, H2CO, CH3OH, and high-redshift low-J CO, HCN, HCO+), combined with radio continuum measurements to constrain gas mass, kinematics, turbulence, and inflow/outflow signatures.
AI.result: SKA surveys will enable detailed studies of feedback-regulated cold gas reservoirs and population-level studies of AGN-driven feedback in radio galaxies, providing direct constraints on multiphase gas flows and feedback energetics.
AI.conclusion: SKA will provide a new framework for understanding how radio jets regulate the cold interstellar medium and star formation across cosmic time, significantly advancing our understanding of AGN feedback mechanisms.

title: Diffuse HI emission in the circumgalactic medium of NGC891 and NGC4565 - III: azimuthal profiles
comment: Accepted to ApJ. 18 pages and 9 figures
summary: Diffuse HI emission in the circumgalactic medium (CGM) of NGC891 and NGC4565 has been previously shown to trace an inflow along minor axes pointings and to co-rotate with the HI disk along major axes pointings out to ~100 kpc (Das2020b,Das2024a). To obtain a 360$^\circ$ view of the inner neutral CGM ($\rm < 25 kpc$ for NGC891, $\rm < 30 kpc$ for NGC4565), we perform deep stare observations with the Green Bank Telescope (GBT) along the off-axes, 45$^\circ$ between principal axes, achieving a 5$σ$ column density sensitivity of $1.1-1.2 x 10^{17} \rm cm^{-2}$ over a 20 kms$^{-1}$ velocity width. While detecting HI emission in the inner CGM with single-dish telescopes is common, separating the true CGM emission from disk contamination is extremely challenging and has so far been largely unsuccessful. To achieve that, we compare our single-dish detections to deep interferometric maps from the Westerbork Synthesis Radio Telescope (WSRT) HALOGAS survey, and improve upon our previous methods by incorporating velocity offset corrections and channel-wise brightness-temperature scaling. We find that $30-38$ % and $18-28$ % of the emission detected by the GBT cannot be explained by WSRT in NGC891 and NGC4565, respectively, implying a true CGM detection. There is $4-6$ ($3-7$) times more HI along the off-axes than major (minor) axes, nullifying the common assumption of azimuthal symmetry of the neutral CGM. The velocity profile of the diffuse inner CGM suggests a lagged co-rotation with the HI disk in both galaxies. This exercise illustrates the power of deep observation and careful cross-instrument comparisons to characterize the diffuse HI in the CGM.

AI.tldr: This paper presents deep GBT single-dish observations of diffuse HI in the inner circumgalactic medium (CGM) of NGC891 and NGC4565 along off-axes (45° between principal axes). By comparing with WSRT HALOGAS interferometric maps using improved velocity-offset corrections and channel-wise brightness-temperature scaling, the authors separate true CGM emission from disk contamination, finding 30-38% and 18-28% of GBT-detected emission is true CGM in each galaxy respectively. The HI distribution is 4-6× more abundant along off-axes than major/minor axes, breaking azimuthal symmetry, and the velocity profiles indicate lagged co-rotation with the HI disk.
AI.motivation: Previous studies mapped diffuse HI in the CGM of NGC891 and NGC4565 along minor axes (inflow) and major axes (co-rotation) out to~100 kpc. To obtain a complete 360° view of the inner neutral CGM, off-axis observations are needed, but separating true CGM emission from disk contamination in single-dish data has been a major unsolved challenge.
AI.method: Deep stare observations with the Green Bank Telescope (GBT) along off-axes (45° between principal axes) achieving 5σ column density sensitivity of 1.1-1.2×10^17 cm^-2 over 20 km/s. Comparison of single-dish GBT detections with deep interferometric WSRT HALOGAS maps, incorporating improved velocity-offset corrections and channel-wise brightness-temperature scaling to isolate true CGM emission from disk contamination.
AI.result: 30-38% of GBT emission in NGC891 and 18-28% in NGC4565 cannot be explained by WSRT interferometric data, implying genuine CGM detections. There is 4-6× more HI along off-axes than major axes and 3-7× more than minor axes, nullifying azimuthal symmetry. Velocity profiles suggest lagged co-rotation with the HI disk in both galaxies.
AI.conclusion: The neutral CGM is not azimuthally symmetric, showing enhanced HI along off-axis directions. The diffuse inner CGM exhibits lagged co-rotation with the disk, and this work demonstrates the power of combining deep single-dish observations with careful cross-instrument comparison to characterize diffuse HI in the CGM.
